byline: Kerith Hartmann, PA-C, Advocacy, Success, and Impact Officer, SAMPA
description: When Jim Anderson started in SAMPA, formerly (and fondly) called SPAAM, it was little more than a spark of an idea.
paragraphs: When Jim Anderson started in SAMPA, formerly (and fondly) called SPAAM, it was little more than a spark of an idea. It was a small, unincorporated group run by a handful of people who cared deeply about the work and the patients it serves. Through years of steady effort, he planted the seeds of what would become a growing professional community. Now, after more than 25 years as a PA in addiction medicine, Jim is nearing retirement. “I am now stepping out of the building, as it were,” he says, “but it has been an honor to work with my patients and my PA, NP, and MSW colleagues, and to watch them blossom over that time.”

Under Shani Wilson’s leadership, SAMPA has since incorporated and become the national organization representing PAs in addiction medicine. In its current form SAMPA is still young, but it is growing quickly, welcoming 39 new members and 177 new weekly newsletter subscribers in the last 6 months. Ask Shani or Jim what drives them, and they will say less about what they have accomplished (which is tremendous) and more about the people they serve and how this work has shaped them.
I checked in with both of them to learn what brought them to this work, what keeps them in it, and what they would tell others considering a career in addiction medicine.

Like many of us, Shani came to this work through personal experience. “My family, like many others, has been affected by this crisis,” she says. “I have lost family members to substance use.” Growing up with an uncle living with AIDS and substance use in the early nineties, she witnessed two of the most stigmatizing conditions of that time, all at once. “He was an amazing man,” she remembers. “He was a wonderful person, a superb cook, and a loving father. As a child, I saw firsthand how much medication he had to take to stay alive. The top of his dresser was completely filled with medication.”  After he died, she turned her grief into a drive to help others. Any judgment she might have carried became empathy instead, which is demonstrated daily in her patient care.

Jim found his calling as a PA student in 2000, during a one-month clinical rotation at Evergreen Treatment Services in Seattle. “I happened across some amazing preceptors, including PAs, NPs, and MSWs,” he recalls. “I knew when I was there that this was where I needed to be. And this is where I spent most of my 25 years as a PA.”

Over the years, Jim recalls a pivotal moment that shaped his practice – the loss of a long-term patient whose recovery was real, even though an unexpected accident cut their life short. “One of my long-term patients really struggled in her efforts to stop using opioids,” Jim says. “She was vigilant, and I really enjoyed working with her. After a few years, something clicked. She was able to stop using opioids, settle into her methadone dose, and get her life back together.” The patient’s path was not linear but with persistence, the stability that methadone provided (Mattick et al., 2009), and a therapeutic relationship Jim describes as a driving force, the patient achieved recovery. “This [patients’ death] was one of the toughest moments of my clinical career,” Jim says. “But I never forgot her hard work to get to where she was, and she taught me so much.” In telling this story, Jim names the grief so many of us feel when we lose a patient. And by naming it, he gives us permission to grieve and to acknowledge our own losses.

Stories like these break down stereotypes and remind us that substance use truly touches everyone. But there is an important distinction we can’t overlook: the consequences of substance use disorder are not shared equally. Consider two patients, one with financial means and insurance and one without. The second is far more likely to face punitive consequences or to go without care altogether. Among adults who feel they need treatment but don’t receive it, being unable to afford care is a more common barrier for those without insurance (Ali et al., 2017). Communities of color have also long faced harsher consequences for the same behavior. For example, from 1980 onward, Black adults were arrested on drug charges at roughly three to five and a half times the rate of White adults (Human Rights Watch, 2009). This is despite the fact that Black and White Americans use substances at similar rates.

Jim recalls that much of SAMPA’s early work involved partnering with like-minded groups to build shared policy agendas. The organization connected with the AAPA LGBTQ Caucus, PAs in Latino Health, and the African American PA Caucus. While there is great diversity in each with distinct histories and needs, Jim saw a common thread among them. Today, Shani carries that commitment forward. She continues to build SAMPA’s partnerships, understanding that broad coalitions carry more weight in policy than single-issue groups.

When I asked Shani what keeps her in the field, her answer was straightforward “It’s the people and the medicine.” She sees addiction care as more than medications for substance use disorder and formal treatment. “It’s never just about substance use,” she explains. “There’s mental health, medical issues, housing, relationships, access to care, and so many other things affecting someone’s health.” What she finds most rewarding is the change she sees in her patients over time. “Watching someone become healthier and more stable, and knowing you played a part in helping them get there, is an amazing feeling,” she says. “I’m grateful for all my patients, and I have witnessed amazing transformations over the years.”

Shani also knows that recovery is not linear. For instance, no one would stop treating a patient with diabetes or hypertension because their numbers went up, and patients with substance use disorder deserve the same treatment persistence. The research supports this non-linearity. Adherence to medication and relapse rates are similar for substance use as they are for chronic illnesses such as type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and asthma. The conclusion? That addiction should be insured, treated, and evaluated just like any chronic illness (McLellan et al., 2000).
Finally, I asked both what advice they would give to PAs who are starting out in addiction medicine or considering the field.

Shani encourages new PAs to listen with curiosity. “Listen to understand, not to judge,” she says. “Learning to understand means recognizing how harm reduction, mental health, trauma, and everything else in someone’s life can impact their recovery. Meet people where they are. Sometimes progress will look very different from what you expected, and that’s ok.”

Jim sees the most pressing issues as removing obstacles that keep interested PAs from entering the field.  “There has been great change and progress for PAs in addiction medicine, and I encourage all PAs with an interest in addiction medicine to consider working in this arena,” he says. “There are plenty of gaps in care and so many places for PAs to step in. Pay for PAs in addiction medicine is improving, and I think there is no arena more rewarding. PAs early and late in their careers can lift up those burdened by opioid use disorder.”

Our board, me included, have benefited from Shani’s thoughtful way of communicating. She brings a grounded professionalism to every discussion and deeply pays attention to every part of the organization as it grows. Jim, for his part, is humble about his contributions. He is quick to point out that none of this would have been possible without the advocacy of those with whom he worked, including his long-term collaborator, Bernard Stuetz. With that, we tip our hats to Jim and Shani, and everyone whose work, seen and unseen, helped build SAMPA into what it is today.

McLellan, A. T., Lewis, D. C., O’Brien, C. P., & Kleber, H. D. (2000). Drug dependence, a chronic medical illness: Implications for treatment, insurance, and outcomes evaluation. JAMA, 284(13), 1689–1695.
